definition: AI Snake Oil: What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can't, and How to Tell the Difference is a 2024 non-fiction book written by scholars Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor.
details: It is a critique of the tech industry's overly inflated promises and capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) as well as a debunking of the flawed science fueling AI hype while attempting to outline both the potential positives and negatives that come with different modes of the technology.

explainer.lead: AI snake oil is Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor’s term for AI that does not and cannot work as advertised. Their 2024 book helps readers separate useful systems from inflated promises by examining predictive AI, generative AI, content moderation, and claims about artificial general intelligence.

tiers.eli5: Imagine someone selling a bottle of medicine that promises to cure everything but cannot actually cure you. AI snake oil is similar: a computer system is said to do something amazing, but it cannot deliver on that promise. The book teaches readers to look past the exciting sales pitch and ask what the system really does.
tiers.practitioner: Use the idea as a review question: what exactly was the system advertised to do, and does evidence show that it works in deployment? For predictive AI, check reproducibility and leakage, where models are tested on their training data; for generative AI and moderation, examine failures involving context, nuance, discrimination, and harmful content. Do not treat a convincing demonstration or a company’s description of a model as sufficient evidence.
tiers.paperLevel: In Narayanan and Kapoor’s usage, AI snake oil is “AI that does not and cannot work as advertised,” with particular attention to overestimated predictive capabilities. Their 2024 book, AI Snake Oil: What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can’t, and How to Tell the Difference, examines failure cases, leakage, irreproducibility, and hidden human labour. It does not claim that all AI is ineffective, and its discussion of AGI leaves future advances on the Ladder of Generality undetermined.

explainer.example: The book discusses six Black people who were falsely arrested because of errors in AI facial-recognition tools. This makes the snake-oil test concrete: an advertised identification capability fails in practice, and the consequences extend far beyond a misleading demonstration.

usedIn.name: Allstate predictive AI
usedIn.detail: The company’s 2013 use of predictive AI is one of the book’s introductory examples.

usedIn.name: Facial recognition
usedIn.detail: Errors in these tools are discussed in connection with the false arrests of six Black individuals.

usedIn.name: ChatGPT, Midjourney, and DALL-E
usedIn.detail: These generative systems illustrate both positive uses and harms, including deepfakes and threats to artistic property.

usedIn.name: Content moderation
usedIn.detail: Fingerprint matching and machine learning are examined alongside problems with context, nuance, discrimination, and shadow banning.

explainer.intuition: A system can sound impressive while failing at the job promised for it. The central test is not whether it uses AI, but whether its advertised capability survives scrutiny of real results, failure cases, and supporting evidence.
howItWorks: State precisely what the AI system claims it can do.
Compare that claim with demonstrated performance and real-world failures.
Check for leakage, irreproducible research, and undisclosed model details.
Examine context, discrimination, harmful outputs, and hidden human labour.
Trace hype to incentives among companies, journalists, and researchers.
explainer.whyItMatters: Overstated capability can turn technical errors into false arrests, discriminatory moderation, or harmful deepfakes. Looking past hype also reveals weak research practices, corporate and media incentives, and the extensive human labour needed to make AI technologies function.
misconceptions: The term does not mean every AI system is fraudulent or useless; the book also discusses positive uses.
Fluent generative output is not evidence that predictive AI can forecast the future or that moderation systems understand nuance.
Skepticism about AGI is not a claim that future advances are impossible; the next rungs of the Ladder of Generality remain undetermined.
